questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: She had prepared extensively for the interview; ______ she didn't get the job.
questions.explanation: After a semicolon we need a conjunctive adverb of contrast: nevertheless = in spite of that. "Whereas" and "albeit" are conjunctions and cannot follow a semicolon this way.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: He practiced his lines diligently, ______ he forgot them during the performance.
questions.explanation: Two clauses joined by a comma need a coordinating conjunction: yet = but. "However", "even so" and "still" are adverbs and would need a semicolon.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: John was determined to finish the marathon, even though he had injured his ankle early on in the race, and he pushed through the pain ______.
questions.explanation: "Pushed through the pain regardless" = despite everything, anyway. "Irrespective" needs "of"; "notwithstanding" normally precedes or follows a noun it governs; "however" would need a comma.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: I would rather you ______ my message to him yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Would rather + subject + past perfect" expresses a wish about the past ("yesterday").

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Not only ______ to the party, but he also brought a gift.
questions.explanation: A sentence starting with "Not only" takes subject–auxiliary inversion; the past tense ("brought") requires did he come.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Bananas are one of ______ and they are believed to help raise serotonin levels.
questions.explanation: Superlative + noun + "available" as a post-modifying adjective: "one of the most nutritious fruits available".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: In no way ______ to be misunderstood.
questions.explanation: A negative adverbial ("In no way") at the front forces inversion with an auxiliary: does she want.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The art exhibit featured a variety of sculptures, each ______ with precision by a renowned artist.
questions.explanation: A reduced passive participle clause: "each (of which was) crafted with precision by…".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: It is important that she ______ her passport before traveling.
questions.explanation: "It is important that + subject + bare infinitive" (present subjunctive): renew.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: After the financial crisis, many families were reduced ______ in temporary shelters, struggling to rebuild their lives from scratch.
questions.explanation: "Be reduced to + V-ing" = be forced into a worse state: "reduced to living in temporary shelters".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Demands for tickets were high, ______ inflating resell prices to 300%.
questions.explanation: "Thereby + V-ing" = by that means, introducing the result of the preceding clause.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: One of the students was caught ______ during the exam and was removed from the room.
questions.explanation: "Catch somebody doing something" — the passive keeps the V-ing form: "was caught cheating".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The company is said ______ victory over its rival through a smear campaign.
questions.explanation: "Is said to have achieved": a perfect infinitive because the achievement is already complete.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Nobody is really what they seem, ______?
questions.explanation: "Nobody" is negative and takes the plural pronoun "they", so the tag is positive: are they?

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ______, the acrobat couldn't make the final landing gracefully.
questions.explanation: "Much to our disappointment" is the fixed phrase for a result that disappoints; "Disappointed as we were" would dangle, since the subject is the acrobat.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The cult leader, along with his 2 closest associates, ______ a life sentence.
questions.explanation: The subject is "The cult leader" (singular — "along with" does not change agreement) and "was to receive" = was due to receive.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: ______ your school uniform? We're just going to the mall with our classmates.
questions.explanation: "Need you have worn…?" questions whether a past action was necessary — it was unnecessary because they are only going to the mall.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Max cheated his sister out of the inheritance money, ______ she would never forgive him.
questions.explanation: "Forgive someone for something" → preposition + relative pronoun: "for which she would never forgive him".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Your road to recovery is likely long. ______, you have the best healthcare service available right now.
questions.explanation: "That said" is the absolute phrase used to introduce a qualification of the previous statement; it needs no subject, unlike the participle form.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Potential delays ______, this airline service isn't so bad.
questions.explanation: "Notwithstanding" can follow the noun it governs: "Potential delays notwithstanding" = despite potential delays.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: After working for several hours straight, Sarah was ______ and needed to take a break.
options: hitting the nail on the head
questions.explanation: "Run out of steam" = lose energy or enthusiasm.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The politician's promise to lower taxes turned out to be nothing but ______.
questions.explanation: "Hot air" = empty talk, promises that mean nothing.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The chef prepared a ______ feast, featuring a variety of delicious dishes.
questions.explanation: "Mouth-watering" describes food that looks or smells delicious.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The media has been reporting non-stop about this scandal for weeks. It's time to stop ______.
questions.explanation: "Flog a dead horse" = keep going over something that is already finished or pointless.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Enjoy your holiday and keep me ______ about anything exciting!
questions.explanation: "Keep someone posted" = keep someone informed of the latest news.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: You have been having terrible luck, I suggest you ______ and stop playing.
questions.explanation: "Cut your losses" = stop doing something before you lose even more.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: These ______ office cubicles are drab, plain, and depressing to work in.
questions.explanation: "Cookie-cutter" = identical and unoriginal, matching "drab, plain".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: That's not very prim and ______ of her to chew with her mouth wide open.
questions.explanation: The fixed binomial is "prim and proper" = very correct in manners.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: I'm sorry, but I have to ______ my plans for tonight due to unexpected circumstances.
questions.explanation: "Put off" = postpone; you postpone plans because of unexpected circumstances.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The company decided to ______ 50 employees in order to reduce costs.
questions.explanation: "Lay off" = dismiss workers, typically to cut costs.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The teacher asked the students to finish and ______ their assignments by Friday.
questions.explanation: "Hand in" = submit work to a teacher.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: She had to ______ the courage to speak in front of such a large audience.
questions.explanation: "Summon (up) the courage" is the collocation for gathering one's courage.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The board was unconvinced by the idea at first, but after the demonstration, most of them ______.
questions.explanation: "Come round" = change your mind and agree after initial reluctance.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Mickey is not telling us the whole story. There's more than he ______.
questions.explanation: "Let on" = reveal a secret; "more than he lets on" is the idiom.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Even though the house was built just a year ago, we are starting to see signs of paint ______ off.
questions.explanation: Paint "chips off" (or peels/flakes off) when small pieces break away.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The highway accident led to a terrible ______ of over 50 vehicles and 100 casualties including deaths.
questions.explanation: A "pileup" is a crash involving many vehicles.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: She ______ her gratitude for the opportunity to work on such an important project.
questions.explanation: "Extend one's gratitude/thanks" = offer or express thanks formally.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The students eagerly participated in a ______, discussing various aspects of the novel.
questions.explanation: Eager participation and discussing "various aspects of the novel" describe a lively debate, not a quarrel or small talk.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The team's ______ performance in the playoffs ended their tournament run prematurely.
questions.explanation: "Lackluster performance" = dull and uninspired, the standard collocation for a poor showing.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: A.I. is bringing about a ___ shift in what is normally considered 'skilled, intellectual, creative' fields.
questions.explanation: "Paradigm shift" = a fundamental change in approach.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: It is ____ normal to live with your parents. You don't have to move out if you don't have the means.
questions.explanation: "Absolutely normal" = completely normal; "utterly" collocates with negative adjectives.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Read your contract carefully before signing as the terms in there are legally ______.
questions.explanation: "Legally binding" = enforceable by law, the fixed collocation for contract terms.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Skeptics ____ to the view that 'alternative medicine' is just placebo without any medicinal properties.
questions.explanation: "Subscribe to a view" = agree with or support an opinion.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The company decided to ______ a new marketing strategy to boost sales and attract more customers.
questions.explanation: "Implement a strategy" = put a plan into action.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The hiker had to ______ a steep mountain to reach the summit.
questions.explanation: To reach the summit you must ascend (climb up) the mountain.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The detective's keen observation skills helped him ______ the mystery behind the missing diamond.
questions.explanation: "Unravel a mystery" = solve it by working out the tangled details.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The author's prose is ____, so even first-time readers of the genre find it easy to follow the story.
questions.explanation: "Lucid" = clearly expressed and easy to understand, matching "easy to follow".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The Amazon rainforest ______ over 3 million species of plants and animals, many of which unique to the region and under serious threat.
questions.explanation: "Boast" = have something impressive: "the rainforest boasts over 3 million species".

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: The striking laborers ______ demands regarding their working conditions, healthcare, and paid leave.
questions.explanation: "Stipulate demands" = state them clearly as conditions.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 1-50 Grammar and Vocabulary
questions.q: Most humans are instinctively ______ to snakes, which are a danger to our primate ancestors.
questions.explanation: "Averse to" = having a strong dislike of; "adverse" means harmful and does not take "to" with a person as subject.

questions.part: I. LANGUAGE USE (4.0 pts) – Questions 51-60 Guided Cloze Test
questions.q: (51) goes the famous rhyme that ______ the fates of King Henry VIII's six wives.
questions.explanation: "Recount" = tell a story or describe events; the rhyme tells the fates of the six wives.
questions.passage:
'Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived' goes the famous rhyme that (51)____ the fates of King Henry VIII's six wives. The story of King Henry VIII's six wives has been told for centuries, but never before has it been heard in the way 'SIX' shares it. A new Broadway musical show, 'SIX' gives (52)____ and tune to the women who served as queens in a modern and upbeat way.

Telling the story of King Henry's wives, some of whom were killed by order of the king himself, the show does not, however, feature a character playing the king. (53)____, it is centered on the women, allowing them to tell their own stories through music.

The entire 80-minute production takes place on a (54)____ that appears to be a concert stage. The Tudor queens and the band, known as the 'Ladies in Waiting,' are on stage the entire time. Despite being based on historical events and characters, 'SIX's take on the Tudor era is heavily fictionalized. (55)____ is clear the moment the actresses stepped out in bejeweled and glittering outfits, and the stage, with modern (56)____ like bass guitar and keyboard, feels more at home at a pop concert than a historical play.

"It can catch you off guard," said Sterlyn Termine, a band member. "As soon as the curtains open and you see guitar, a drum set and keyboards, you will realize that this is going to sound a lot more modern than you thought." Still, (57)____ the era and region the storyline takes place in, there are hints of the music from 500 years ago. "There is harpsichord, but it is a synthesized harpsichord, and one of the songs is polka, German-folk inspired that is accompanied by dubstep and airhorn sounds. It is a creative and clever fusion," Termine said. Each queen also has hints of modern-day celebrities, dubbed 'Queenspirations,' with their music, intertwined into their characters and songs, paying (58)____ to 'pop queens' the likes of Beyoncé, Adele, and Ariana Grande.

The show is high energy from start to finish and does not include an intermission. Many of the (59)____ loved how it was fast-paced and shorter than some other productions, adding that though they didn't know what to expect (60)____ the show, they left highly impressed. "We thought we booked the wrong show, but as the curtains closed, me and my family were all clapping and cheering." Said a member in attendance.

(Dillon Thomas, for CBS News)

questions.q: What is the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: Traffic safety officer: Challenges and Opportunities
How cars have lost their status as 'king of the road'
questions.explanation: The whole passage is about Monderman removing signs, lights and markings ("shared space") and the roads becoming safer as a result.
questions.passage:
A. Like a naturalist conducting a tour of the jungle, he led the way to a busy intersection in the center of town, where several odd things immediately became clear. Not only was it virtually naked, stripped of all lights, signs, and road markings, but there was no division between road and sidewalk. It was, basically, a bare brick square.

But in spite of the apparently anarchical layout, the traffic, a steady stream of trucks, cars, buses, motorcycles, bicycles, and pedestrians, moved along fluidly and easily, as if directed by an invisible conductor. When Mr. Monderman, a traffic engineer and the intersection's proud designer, deliberately failed to check for oncoming traffic before crossing the street, the drivers slowed for him. No one honked or shouted rude words out of the window. (1)"Who has the right of way?" he asked rhetorically. "I don't care. People here have to find their own way, negotiate for themselves, use their own brains."

B. Used by some 20,000 drivers a day, the intersection is part of a road-design revolution pioneered by the 59-year-old Mr. Monderman. His work in Friesland, the district in northern Holland that takes in Drachten, is increasingly seen as the way of the future in Europe.

His philosophy is simple, if counterintuitive. To make communities safer and more appealing, Mr. Monderman argues, you should first remove the traditional paraphernalia of their roads-the traffic lights and speed signs; the signs exhorting drivers to stop, slow down and merge; the center lines separating lanes from one another; even the speed bumps, speed-limit signs, bicycle lanes, and pedestrian crossings. In his view, it is only when the road is made more dangerous, when drivers stop looking at signs and start looking at other people, that driving becomes safer.

"All those signs are saying to cars, 'This is your space, and we have organized your behavior so that as long as you behave this way, nothing can happen to you,'" Mr. Monderman said. "That is the wrong story." The Drachten intersection is an example of the concept of "shared space," a street where cars and pedestrians are equal, and the design tells the driver what to do. "It's moving away from regulated, legislated traffic toward space which, by the way it's designed and configured, makes it clear what sort of behavior is anticipated," said Ben Hamilton-Baillie, a British specialist in urban design and movement and a proponent of many of the same concepts.

Highways, where the car is naturally king, are part of the "traffic world" and another matter altogether. In Mr. Monderman's view, shared-space schemes thrive only in conjunction with well-organized, well-regulated highway systems. Variations on the shared-space theme are being tried in Spain, Denmark, Austria, Sweden, and Britain, among other places. The European Union has appointed a committee of experts, including Mr. Monderman, for a Europe-wide study.

C. Mr. Monderman is a man on a mission. On a daylong automotive tour of Friesland, he pointed out places he had improved, including a town where he ripped out the sidewalks, signs, and crossings and put in brick paving on the central shopping street. An elderly woman crossed slowly in front of him. (2)"This is social space, so when Grandma is coming, you stop, because that's what normal, courteous human beings do," he said.

Planners and curious journalists are increasingly making pilgrimages to meet Mr. Monderman, considered one of the field's great innovators, although until a few years ago he was virtually unknown outside Holland. Mr. Hamilton-Baillie, whose writings have helped bring Mr. Monderman's work to wider attention, remembers with fondness his own first visit. Mr. Monderman drove him to a small country road with cows in every direction. Their presence was reinforced by a large, standard-issue European traffic sign with a picture of a cow on it.

He said: "What do you expect to find here? Wallabies??" Mr. Hamilton-Baillie recalled. "They're treating you like you're a complete idiot, and if people treat you like a complete idiot, you'll act like one."

D. Here was someone who had rethought a lot of issues from complete scratch. Essentially, what it means is a transfer of power and responsibility from the state to the individual and the community. Dressed in a beige jacket and patterned shirt, with scruffy facial hair and a stocky build, Mr. Monderman has the appearance of a football hooligan, but the temperament of an engineer, which indeed he trained to be. His father was the headmaster of the primary school in their small village; Hans liked to fiddle with machines. "I was always the guy who repaired the TV sets in our village," he said. He was working as a civil engineer building highways in the 1970s when the Dutch government, alarmed at a sharp increase in traffic accidents, set up a network of traffic safety offices. Mr. Monderman was appointed Friesland's traffic safety officer.

In residential communities, Mr. Monderman began narrowing the roads and putting in design features like trees and flowers, red brick paving stones, and even fountains to discourage people from speeding, following the principle now known as psychological traffic calming, where behavior follows design.

He made his first nervous foray into shared space in a small village whose residents were upset at its being used as a daily thoroughfare for 6,000 speeding cars. When he took away the signs, lights, and sidewalks, people drove more carefully. Within two weeks, speeds on the road had dropped by more than half. In fact, he said, there has never been a fatal accident on any of his roads.

E. Several early studies bear out his contention that shared spaces are safer. In England, the district of Wiltshire found that removing the center line from a stretch of road reduced drivers' speed without any increase in accidents.

[...] Mr. Monderman concedes that road design can do only so much. It does not change the behavior, for instance, of the 15 percent of drivers who will behave badly no matter what the rules are. Nor are shared-space designs appropriate everywhere, like major urban centers, but only in neighborhoods that meet particular criteria. Recently a group of well-to-do parents asked him to widen the two-lane road leading to their children's school, saying it was too small to accommodate what he derisively calls "their huge cars." He refused, saying the fault was not with the road, but with the cars. (3)"They can't wait for each other to pass?" he asked. [...]

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the "digital program" view came "much later" than Locke and Hume, and only "more recently" did scientists argue the mind "works by storing records of actual experiences" — so the software view came first.
questions.passage:
'GOOD VIDEO GAMES AND GOOD LEARNING' – James P. Gee

Video games are a relatively new technology replete with important, and not yet fully understood, implications. Scholars have historically viewed the human mind through the lens of a technology they thought worked like the mind. Locke and Hume, for example, argued that the mind was like a blank slate on which experience wrote ideas, taking the technology of literacy as their guide. Much later, modern cognitive scientists argued that the mind worked like a digital program, calculating generalizations and deductions via a logic-like rule system. More recently, some cognitive scientists, inspired by distributed parallel-processing computers and complex adaptive networks, have argued that the mind works by storing records of actual experiences and constructing intricate patterns of connections among them.

Human societies get better through history at building technologies that more closely capture some of what the human mind can do and getting these technologies to do mental work publicly. Writing, digital computers, and networks each allow us to externalize some functions of the mind. Though they are not commonly thought of in these terms, video games are a new technology in this same line. They are a new tool with which to think about the mind and through which we can externalize some of its functions. Video games of the sort I am concerned with—games like Half-Life 2, Rise of Nations, Full Spectrum Warrior, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, and World of WarCraft—are what I would call "action-and-goal-directed preparations for, and simulations of, embodied experience."

Human understanding is not primarily a matter of storing general concepts in the head or applying abstract rules to experience. Rather, humans think and understand best when they can imagine (simulate) an experience in such a way that the simulation prepares them for actions they need and want to take in order to accomplish their goals. Let's take weddings as an example, though we could just as well have taken war, love, inertia, democracy, or anything. You don't understand the word or the idea of weddings by meditating on some general definition of weddings. Rather, you have had experiences of weddings, in real life and through texts and media. On the basis of these experiences, you can simulate different wedding scenarios in your mind.

You construct these simulations differently for different occasions, based on what actions you need to take to accomplish specific goals in specific situations. You can move around as a character in the mental simulation as yourself, imagining your role in the wedding, or you can "play" other characters at the wedding (e.g., the minister), imagining what it is like to be that person. You build your simulations to understand and make sense of things, but also to help you prepare for action in the world. You can act in the simulation and test out what consequences follow, before you act in the real world. You can role-play another person in the model and try to see what motivates their actions or might follow from them before you respond in the real world. So I am arguing that the mind is a simulator, but one that builds simulations to purposely prepare for specific actions and to achieve specific goals.

Video games turn out to be the perfect metaphor for what this view of the mind amounts to, just as slates and computers were good metaphors for earlier views of the mind. Video games usually involve a visual and auditory world in which the player manipulates a virtual character (or characters). They often come with editors or other sorts of software with which the player can make changes to the game world or even build a new game world. The player can make a new landscape, a new set of buildings, or new characters. The player can set up the world so that certain sorts of actions are allowed or disallowed. The player is building a new world, but is doing so by using and modifying the original visual images that came with the game. One simple example of this is the way in which players can build new skateboard parks in a game like Tony Hawk Pro Skater. The player must place ramps, trees, grass, poles, and other things in space in such a way that players can manipulate their virtual characters to skate the park in a fun and challenging way.

Even when players are not modifying games, they play them with goals in mind, the achievement of which counts as their "win state," and it's the existence of such win states that, in part, distinguishes games from other simulations. These goals are set by the player, but certainly, in collaboration with the world the game designers have created, and, at least in more open-ended games, players don't just accept developer's goals, they make real choices of their own. Players must carefully consider the design of the world and consider how it will or will not facilitate specific actions they want to take to accomplish their goals. One technical way that psychologists have talked about this sort of situation is through the notion of 'affordances'. An 'affordance' is a feature of the world (real or virtual) that will allow for a certain action to be taken, but only if it is matched by an ability in an actor who has the wherewithal to carry out such an action. For example, in the massive multiplayer game World of WarCraft stags can be killed and skinned (for making leather), but only by characters that have learned the 'Skinning' skill. So a stag is an affordance for skinning for such a player, but not for one who has not acquired said skill. The large spiders in the game are not an affordance for skinning for any players, since they cannot be skinned at all. Affordances are relationships between the world and actors. Playing World of WarCraft, or any other video game, is all about such affordances. The player must learn to see the game world—designed by the developers, but set in motion in particular directions by the players, and, thus, co-designed by them—in terms of such affordances. Broadly speaking, players must utilize their resources and think in terms of "What are the features of this world that can enable the actions I am capable of carrying out and that I want to carry out in order to achieve my goals?"

The view of the mind I have sketched, in fact, argues that the mind works rather like a video game. For humans, effective thinking is more like running a simulation than it is about forming abstract generalizations cut off from experiential realities. Generalizations are formed, when they are, bottom up from experience and imagination of experience. Video games externalize the search for affordances, for a match between character (actor) and world, but this is just the heart and soul of effective human thinking and learning in any situation.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
For the audience, the effortless performance of the acrobats was astonishing. (HOW)
→ The audience was ______ performed.
accept: astonished at how effortlessly the acrobats
astonished by how effortlessly the acrobats
astonished at how effortlessly the acrobats had
astonished by how effortlessly the acrobats had
questions.answer: astonished at how effortlessly the acrobats
questions.explanation: "Astonished at/by how effortlessly the acrobats performed" — the adjective "effortless" becomes the adverb after "how".

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
Molly told me it is not a good idea to throw away the receipts. (HOLD)
→ 'You had ______.' Molly told me.
accept: better hold on to the receipts
better hold on to your receipts
better hold on to those receipts
questions.answer: better hold on to the receipts
questions.explanation: "You had better hold on to the receipts" = you should keep them (advice), the opposite of throwing them away.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
Being uncharismatic made it hard for her to become a successful actress. (BARRED)
→ Her lack of ______ success in acting.
questions.explanation: "Her lack of charisma barred her from (achieving) success" — bar somebody from something = prevent them from getting it.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
If we want to finish before the deadline, we have to work faster. (PICK)
→ The deadline cannot ______ the pace.
accept: be met unless we pick up
be met if we don't pick up
be met unless we pick up the pace
be met without us picking up
be met without our picking up
be met unless we pick up on
questions.answer: be met unless we pick up
questions.explanation: "The deadline cannot be met unless we pick up the pace" — pick up the pace = work faster; "unless" = if … not.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
They will do whatever it takes to save the company. (STOP)
→ They will ______ the company going.
accept: stop at nothing in order to keep
stop at nothing so as to keep
questions.explanation: "Stop at nothing to do something" = be willing to do anything to achieve it; "keep the company going" = save it.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
'You must tell me how the money got lost!' the boss demanded. (ACCOUNT)
→ The boss demanded that ______ money.
accept: I should account for the lost
I should account for the missing
we should account for the lost
we should account for the missing
questions.explanation: "Demand that + subject + (should) + bare infinitive": the boss demanded that I account for (explain) the lost money.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
There is a severe shortage of clean water in our community after the disaster. (DIRE)
→ Our community ______ after the disaster.
accept: is in dire need of clean water
has been in dire need of clean water
is in dire shortage of clean water
is in dire straits for clean water
questions.answer: is in dire need of clean water
questions.explanation: "Be in dire need of something" = need it urgently; a severe shortage means the community badly needs clean water.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
The economy is in crisis, so it is very likely that many companies will go bankrupt. (VERGE)

on the verge of going bankrupt due
on the verge of bankruptcy owing
on the verge of going bankrupt owing

on the verge of going bankrupt thanks

questions.explanation: "On the verge of bankruptcy / going bankrupt" = very close to it; "due to" gives the cause.

questions.part: III. WRITING (3.5 pts) – Questions 121-130 Sentence Transformation
questions.q:
The manager covered up the mistake because he didn't want to be criticized. (FEAR)
→ The manager swept the mistake ______ criticism.
accept: under the carpet for fear of
under the rug for fear of
under the carpet out of fear of
under the rug out of fear of
under the carpet in fear of
under the rug in fear of
questions.answer: under the carpet for fear of
questions.explanation: "Sweep something under the carpet" = cover it up; "for fear of criticism" = because he was afraid of being criticized.

questions.q:
The touring company stopped to have some food before continuing their journey. (BITE)

had a bite, the touring company continued
